clinicalPearls: Presents as bilateral, symmetrical, painless, soft enlargement of the salivary glands, most often the parotids
It is a non-inflammatory, non-neoplastic condition and the glands are typically non-tender with normal overlying skin
Strongly associated with systemic and metabolic disorders, particularly diabetes mellitus, chronic alcohol use, malnutrition, and eating disorders such as bulimia nervosa
Recurrent vomiting in bulimia characteristically produces painless parotid swelling that may be a clue to an otherwise concealed eating disorder
Salivary secretion is often reduced, and diagnosis rests on excluding inflammatory, autoimmune, and neoplastic causes
Imaging shows diffuse, homogeneous gland enlargement without a discrete mass or ductal obstruction
Management is directed at the underlying systemic disorder rather than the gland itself, and the swelling may regress when that condition is controlled
reference.pathophysiology: Sialadenosis is a non-inflammatory, non-neoplastic enlargement of the salivary glands caused by an underlying metabolic or systemic disturbance. It is thought to reflect a peripheral autonomic (sympathetic) neuropathy affecting the secretory acinar cells, leading to dysregulated protein synthesis and secretion. The acinar cells become hypertrophied and engorged with secretory granules, producing diffuse, symmetrical gland enlargement without inflammation or duct obstruction. Recognised associations include diabetes and other endocrine disorders, chronic alcoholism with liver disease, malnutrition, and the repeated vomiting of bulimia nervosa.
additionalInvestigations: Ultrasound of the salivary glands to confirm diffuse enlargement and exclude a focal mass or calculus
Screening for diabetes with fasting glucose or HbA1c
Liver function tests and assessment of alcohol intake
Nutritional assessment and evaluation for an eating disorder where relevant
Autoantibody screen (anti-Ro/anti-La) and salivary flow studies to exclude Sjogren syndrome
Serum IgG4 and, if a mass or atypical features are present, fine-needle aspiration or biopsy
redFlags: A discrete, hard, or asymmetrical mass suggesting neoplasm rather than sialadenosis
Facial nerve weakness accompanying parotid enlargement
Rapid unilateral enlargement or associated lymphadenopathy suggesting lymphoma
Systemic features of an occult malignancy or autoimmune disease
reference.prognosis: Sialadenosis itself is benign; the swelling often persists but may regress if the underlying metabolic or systemic condition is treated. The prognosis is largely determined by the associated disorder, and recognising the swelling can prompt diagnosis of a hidden condition such as an eating disorder.
pitfalls: Mistaking diffuse bilateral swelling for recurrent sialadenitis and giving repeated antibiotics
Overlooking an underlying eating disorder in a patient with painless parotid enlargement
Failing to exclude Sjogren syndrome, lymphoma, or a neoplasm
Attributing gland enlargement solely to the salivary glands without seeking a systemic cause
Proceeding to unnecessary surgery for a benign, systemically driven condition
references: Cummings Otolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery
